speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following interview of Anna Bremner was taped on June 19, 1975 by Dale Anderson at St. Mary's, Idaho. Why don't you just briefly talk about the disadvantages and advantages of rural living as you see it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think it's real good to be out where we can raise a lot of stuff ourselves and it's, we don't have a lot of neighbors around to bother us. We've got some real good neighbors. They're real nice to us. And, I don't know, I just don't think about going back to town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, talk about some of the things that you and your brothers and sisters did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we, like I said, we rode horseback, we went skating, we went swimming. Your brothers and sisters? Yeah. Oh yeah? Yeah, we did in high school. Yeah. Yeah. And, and at Coeur d'Alene, when we were in Coeur d'Alene, we did a lot of swimming. We were right by the lake. And, oh, I don't know. I don't know that we went on so many picnics. We went on more picnics when we were married and had children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you or your brothers or sisters expected to go to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean to college? Right. No, that seemed to be up to whether we wanted to go or not. My sister wanted to be a nurse, but the older one, the younger one, always wanted to. But she didn't have the help to go to be a nurse. And the other one went to Idaho, the University of Idaho. She had a heart condition. But she did... Hers was mostly music. She played the violin. She played the organ. Played the piano. So that was most of her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she do anything with the music? No, because she... Aside from a personal thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because she didn't live long enough. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you go to business school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I suppose about a year and a half.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that the length of the curriculum or did you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it's however long it takes you to go do what you... get what you want done. You know, learn the bookkeeping and the typing and the shorthand.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were the classes structured or was it more or less paced to your individual...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To your own, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were there many people going to the school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, there was quite a few, yes. At that time, that was one of the... I think there were only two business colleges in Spokane back then. Now I don't know that there's more. Of course now I think they go to like junior college, but there is that Kelsey Business College in Spokane.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think I've heard of another one too. Have you? I'm not even sure what the name is, but it seems like I heard that. Okay, why don't you talk about your courtship?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It started in high school. 1912. We lived over in Miltown. My folks lived in Miltown.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where's Miltown?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was way over there. It's way over there on... out of town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How far?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it's... I think... Is it a mile from town, Jeff? About a mile.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does it still exist?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, the mill isn't over there. There's lots of houses over there that were built when we were there. At the time we lived in there, when my mother was over there, they had a little school there. That's where my little younger sister started school. Now there's just houses. People live over there. But I was going to say, we walked the railroad tracks all the time, going back and forth.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just for kicks?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that's the way we... We never got out on the road. We walked the railroad tracks. Now you wouldn't ride... You wouldn't walk a railroad track now, I don't think, because the police would go so fast, Jeff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you mean you walked down the center of the railroad track because that was a nice way to walk? Yeah. And it was clear?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Oh, most of the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the mill was a lumber mill?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And the mill was a lumber mill. And... I guess the thing was that Jim went to Palmer's school the second, and in 1912 and 13 he graduated Palmer. I graduated in 14 at St. Mary's. And I went to business college and he went to... Oh, he was in World War I.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you correspond?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he wasn't a good letter writer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you a good letter writer?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I was a good letter writer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you write him a lot?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not so much. Not when he was overseas.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Had you talked about getting married before he went overseas?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I guess so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You don't remember?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I think we did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long was it after he came back that you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we didn't get married right away. See, he came... When did you come back? 1918? 19... Oh, we got married in 1920.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you working when he came back? Mm-hmm. When did you stop working?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Stopped working to... He was over in Montana. And we came over here and we got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you went back to Montana? Went back to Montana, mm-hmm. And so that was when you quit work? Yeah. What were some of your expectations before marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have a family. I think that was me. Oh, Jim didn't. Jim wanted a family, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many children did you want?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I can't say that... I just wanted a big family and I got it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many children did you have? Seven. Okay. Okay. What medical services did you have when you had your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When the... From the... They had a hospital in St. Mary's and all the children were born in that hospital.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where did you get your knowledge about childbirth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Dr. Cornwallet was here at the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long had he been in St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How long in St. Mary's? Yeah. Since 1911.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long was he your family doctor? Or was he your family doctor?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was the family doctor, yes. But... Well, he... Let me see, I think I had... He lived quite a while, but... I don't know what happened. There wasn't a... He must have been gone someplace when Helen was born because he wasn't there. Dr. Robbins was there. He used to be the governor. He was there at the time that one of them was born. But otherwise, Dr. Cornwall was there all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did you keep the one doctor for most of your life here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Until he died.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you learn about child rearing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I suppose I had a book or two when I... After I got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean about raising a small child? What about just raising children in general as they got older?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I just raised them. I didn't learn it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just whatever came natural? Yeah. Okay. What do you see as the future for your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think they're all doing real good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever put any expectations on them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. I think they do what they want to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever encourage them to go to school? Once they decided, you encouraged them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Now, John, the one boy, went to Gonzaga for two years. But then he got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever push them at home in schoolwork or help them in any way?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. We had to help them a little bit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that at their request? Or did you ever have to sit them down?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. They were pretty good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you read a lot?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't anymore. Well, I have talking books now. Yeah. Before. Before. Yes. I like to read.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your children pick that up from you? Mm-hmm. What do you see in the future for your grandchildren?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know. I know that the ones in North Bend are all doing real good. And there's one, just one, well, no. No, there's one boy who graduated from high school last year and went to the University of Idaho. But he didn't finish his semester because he ran out of money. But then he came home and he went to work at the plywood. He says he's going back. And the other grandchildren seem to be getting married. We had five weddings last year. Grandchildren.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you get together at any of the weddings?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We went to, we were all but one. One was in San, the oldest boy that was in North Bend, that's in Rhode Island now, was married in San Diego and was in the Navy. We went to that one and we went to, and his sister got married in August and we went to that one. And there was, two got married here and one got married in Klamath Falls. We didn't go to that one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many grandchildren do you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Seventeen.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And great-grandchildren? Four. Okay. Do you ever kind of look into the future and see what life might be like in the future for your great-grandchildren?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any thoughts about how lifestyles have changed or how your lifestyle has changed?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't think my lifestyle has changed so much. Because we're, I've longed, you know, like the grandmothers have come, but we don't go very much, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you travel, what about your travels? Early life and now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not too much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about vacations?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we don't take a vacation. Once a, oh, we didn't take one this year. We did go, we have been going over to North Bend every year. But, and we went to San Diego for that wedding, but, you know, to Coeur d'Alene, Jim's sister is down there, and that's about as far as we go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your vacations since you've been married, are those to see relatives or those for your enjoyment?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly to see relatives. Well, that's it. We enjoy that kind of vacation.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Visiting relatives. You have a close family. That's really nice. Do you usually just kind of set aside time during the year, like a week or just...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We have to, we usually do, we had been going to, we were going over to North Bend in the fall, you know, after all the garden was all, but the last year, the year before, we went in the spring. You know, before the fort was time to put the garden in. Oh. We had a, Jim and his sister, that we went to California to, I believe we went, did we go two or three times? I think it was. To see, to visit her. She lived in Oakland. And we enjoyed that. She was, she was, she was a widow. And she took us around lots of places, just lots, we saw a lot of places, and we went down to see her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you enjoy doing that type of traveling? Mm-hmm. What states have you been in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not many.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many years were you in Wisconsin?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, until I was about 13.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you moved.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I never been back there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Really? No. Do you have any family in Wisconsin?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. No, they're gone. They're moved away from us. My mother had a sister that lived, not in, not in River Lake, but she had in, in Medford, Wisconsin. And, but she's gone. And I think all her family, I don't think any of her family was there, has left there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hmm. What about your husband's family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We haven't got many left. We just got, we just hit his sister, Caroline, and himself left with the family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anyone in Michigan, or just everyone? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Idaho? No. In Idaho. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you've been to California, and Oregon, and Washington, and Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Idaho. That's it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you came by train out here. Yeah. How did you travel to the other states?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we, we flew to California. Once we went, the first time I think we went down on the bus. We'd go to North Bend and stop there, and then we went down. Then we went down on the bus, but the other times we flew down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you rather ride the bus or fly?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't like the bus. The only thing about, I think about riding a bus, you see more scenery than flying, but you, but when we went to that wedding, our, our daughter and her husband and one of their boys, we went with them. That was the mother and father of the boy that was getting married. We went, we drove. That was nice trip.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you, what mode of travel do you like the best? Plane, train?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I'd like, I'd like to get on a train again, but I haven't been on one since, oh, when we first came to St. Mary's, it was passengers running through St. Mary's, you know. The only time we, the way we'd get to Spokane would be on a passenger.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many years did you have that service?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't remember how long that service was taking. And then another thing when we were, when we were on first, when we, when we came to St. Mary's, we came up to St. Mary's on, on a boat, the big boats, you know, that came up to St. Mary's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: From Coeur d'Alene?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: From Coeur d'Alene.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Down the river or up the river?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's up the river. I think there's, why don't you get that book, The Way It Was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of boat is it? Was it just a steamboat? Steamboat, uh-huh. With a paddle wheel? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Jim, why don't you get that book, The Way It Was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you like about riding the train?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I liked the train. I think maybe because I'd like to ride it again and they don't have them, you know. I mean, they, like, when the trains used to go through St. Mary's, the passengers. We went to, yeah, they went to, yeah, we went to Seattle. I went to Seattle on the train. We went to Seattle on a train for the Seattle Fair.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go to the Space Needle?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Jim did, but I was, we went to some restaurant and I got sick from what I had to eat there. Down, down the bottom ones, Jim.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go to the fair in Spokane? Uh-huh. Which one did you like the best?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, Spokane was a lot better than Seattle. Really? Oh, my, I should say. And, you know, our daughter had come from North Bend and they'd heard that the fair was no good over here. And our daughter that lives here took them to the fair and they spent a whole day and they just thought it was wonderful. It must be under something, Jim, under a piece, under a tablecloth or something.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you like about the Spokane Fair over the Seattle Fair?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there was more to see and more to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My husband liked the Seattle Fair better than the Spokane Fair. And that was the only one I've ever seen, so I can say. Have you ever been to any other World Fairs? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you better quit looking for it, Jim. It's not in either of the two top drawers, I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you see more countryside in a train versus a bus, or is it about the same?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I imagine it's about the same. About the same. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do now for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we don't do much. We don't, uh, we just go to the meetings of the organizations that we belong to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's about all we do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, once in a while we take a ride up the river. And not on the boat, but we go for a ride and pick up a pickup now, because I don't have a car. But it's easier to drive a picket for somebody like me, because I can drive and sit up higher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you get together with your family. On holidays, mostly? Holidays, birthdays.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We go up there a bit. We've been up to. Oh, show them. Look at the boat. Find the boat for her. Oh, that's good. I'll just turn the page and show them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, an old log cabin. Like this?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I can't see.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's, uh, the Georgie Oaks?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, that's the Georgie Oaks. And there was one called the Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which one were you on?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, there were the Flyer and the Georgie Oaks and the Idaho and the Flyer were the ones that came. They came up from Carlene every day at that time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, all those boats ran the river?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They were on the river, but there was always that big boat that came up to St. Mary. But they had a lot of passengers, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How far down the river did it go? Carlene. From Coeur d'Alene to St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did it go up to St. Joe? Yeah, up to St. Joe. But St. Joe, there's no town there now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's interesting. I want to look at that some more. Okay, why don't you describe what you've done around your house?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Around my house?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, the type of work that you do, your day-to-day life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, well, I used to do a lot of embroidery work, you know, a lot of crocheting and sewing and stuff like that, but I don't do that anymore. It's just ordinary work. It takes me till noon time. We have our dinner at noon time, and it takes me most of the morning to get everything done for dinner. I make a pie, I make bread twice. I make bread every week. I make two loaves and put one loaf in the freezer, and two loaves last a week. Sometimes I have to get a little ahead of that. I make a lot of cookies. I write letters. I have a tape recorder and a cassette. That's what I use a lot for letters now. My typing is going down the drain. So you mail those off? Because I can't see it, huh?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you correspond with old friends, or is it mostly family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about the friends that you had when you were in high school? Are they still in town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there's one. There's just about... Oh, there's a few here, but there's one friend. But she's a businesswoman. She has the credit bureau in St. Mary's, and she's still working.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that Grimner?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that's Margie Smith, but we put that on our name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. I was going to say, I remember you put the name down.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, Margie Smith. That's her. There's a few. Mrs. Scribner is a good friend of mine, but I didn't know her long, like in school. She wasn't here at that time. She came here after she got married. Well, there's a few that I knew, you know, the older people. Well, the church has just changed so much. I mean, there's so many new people here. This plywood people brought plywood, and now the railroad came in. There's just so many new people we don't even know. We're strangers in church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you feel about all the new people coming into the town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's good for the town because I don't think there's so much unemployment in St. Mary's. There's lots of places.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you describe the town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I love the town. The whole town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does everybody feel that way about St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think they do. I think they do. There was one couple that was sitting next to us, and they got up and left. I don't know. They had something to do. They come from California two or three years ago, and they just think St. Mary's is the most friendly town that they ever saw. They lived in lots of places in California, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before the new industries and the new people came in, was St. Mary's a pretty stable town? I mean, were the people who – most of the people had lived here a long time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A long time. Yes, a long time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it just recently that you've had a lot of new people come in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, after the flyaway came in, there have been a lot of new people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know if those people find St. Mary's a friendly town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think they do. A lot of them. I don't know whether everybody does. We don't belong to a lot where we go, like the Elks or the Eagles, where we're around and mix with people like that. I think a lot of people think St. Mary's is a real nice place. There's a lot they can do to St. Mary's, like the streets and things like that. We didn't want to leave. None of our children want to leave. The oldest girl, she was over in Seattle going in nurses' training when she met her husband. He was in the Navy. But they have talked lots of times of coming back to St. Mary's when they retire. They still have two boys. They had one boy graduate from high school this year, and they still have two boys. As long as those boys have children in school, I don't think they'll come because they have that junior college over there. The boys are the whole family of good workers, and they're known to be good workers. There's in North Bend, so I don't think they'll come until, if they ever do, they won't come until after the children are all out of school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long have you lived on this land?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: On this land? Yeah. Since when did you move down here?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We bought that place in 38.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Wasn't it 58 when you sold it? And then you built this house up here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you've been right in this area for a long time. When did you all decide to move out here? And what prompted you to move out here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We thought it was a good place for us to have a family. We have a garden. Jim Light Farm. We own that land up there. Yeah, we own that land. We own lots of land. We had a garden up there. We were going to build a house for it up. It joins this land. It joins this land, uh-huh. But Jim just moved us here on the farm. It was a good place for children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you lived any place since you've been married? Have you lived in another area in St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We lived in town for a while. We lived in town, but not on the... right in town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you own a house there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When we came back from Montana, we built a house out on what they call town site. And, um... well, we sold that and we lived in some other houses, but... This was a good place to... We weren't going to move down there. We were going to move... There was a big house on this place. And it burned down after we were down there. But we were going to build a house up that way, because we owned land up the river quite a ways. But, um... well, the woman that had lived in this house and owned that place, she wanted us to... she was getting old. She wanted us to get down and take over that place. So we went.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you still can very much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Quite a bit. I think about... well, I'd say around thirty-some quarts of applesauce. I think I had more of that than pears. Not too many peaches this last year. We don't eat so many peaches. But we have lots of frozen apples to make pies. You make pies. We make a lot of pies.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have one freezer, too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. We just have a big freezer. A big freezer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Why don't you talk about your community and church activities?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well... The church activities, I'm not so active in church anymore. I go to church all the time. We go to church all the time. But then we just don't belong to... I don't drive anymore, so I can't get to town. Most of the guild meetings are at night. And the group that I did belong to, we met in the afternoon. But, as I said, they got... everybody got a little bit old and we kind of quit. But we did a lot of work for the missions when we belonged to that. And we also belonged to the deanery, which is all the Catholic women in this North Idaho. I don't sew anymore, so I don't do anything in World War I where they make all this... They do all this sewing for the veterans' hospitals. And the Grandmothers' Club. Oh, that's a federated club. They're trying to build a home for grandmothers in... I think it's in Floridak. Well, we really don't do that. We don't pay any attention to that because nobody from this... Make of the woods is going to go to that home down there. But they're going to have a national convention in Portland. I believe it's in September. And there are some of them going to that. But I don't really care about going to those conventions.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever wanted to go outside of the Northwest? Just to visit?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. It would be nice to go. But we don't have... Most of the people we know are right here in the Northwest. Like Jim's sister was in California. She passed away. So there's no one we know to go down there and visit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever been curious about seeing some countryside?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I'd like to see... I would like to have seen countryside before, but it's too late.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of embroidery work did you display at the county fair when you won the award?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it was dish towels or apple pastes. But I did a lot of... I had a lot of embroidery work that I made for my mother. When I was in high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh. Is it mostly pillowcases and towels?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's pillowcases and I have a 54-inch round centerpiece, you know. That's... just got a lot of work on it. Just a lot of work.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you mean? I don't...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Embroidery. Well, I don't know where it is right now. I'll show you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it a piece of... it's a flat piece of work that has...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's a flat piece. It's a circle piece and it's got roses all inside. Embroidered. And then it's what you call scalloping all around. That's what I did a lot of, you know, when I was younger.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you do much tatting?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, quite a bit of tatting years ago, but I haven't tatted for a long, long time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever do any embroidery on your children's clothes?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't think so. I did a lot of knitting, though.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Knit sweaters? Uh-huh. Where did you learn to knit?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. I'm talking... I think probably some Swede woman over in Illinois or Washington probably taught me. When you were... what you were a bookkeeper over there? When I was a bookkeeper, books I would just throw over there. And it was a woman that wire-boarded.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you like being a bookkeeper?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I liked being a bookkeeper.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you like raising a family more? Uh-huh. That's what I thought. Um... where did you learn to crochet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. I was young when I learned to crochet. Now, Mother didn't teach me because she didn't crochet.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about tatting?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Somebody was helping me, but not her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you teach your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they... I don't think I taught them how to tat.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about knitting? Crocheting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And knitting was one... Oh, that one I want to not tell you. She just... she does everything. So this one up here is... taking painting lessons, ceramics. And I never did any of that. But... She does a little... she did do a little knitting. The one... the youngest sister at Cottonwood, she does a lot of knitting. A lot of those sisters at the convent make a lot of... They can sell all the baby things that they can make.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Or crochet. Do you get to see your daughters who are sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Quite often. Since they have changed, you know, they've changed... they've changed a lot. And they... we had one here last week.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So they get to travel.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then we had... The one has her birthday on Jim's birthday, and they were both here in April for the weekend. So they come up quite often. And Margie Smith has one down there, and she drives, and she was coming up to a wedding of her nephew that was to be in Carlisle, and so this daughter of ours came up with her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you both Catholic? Mm-hmm. When you were married, you were both Catholic?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he wasn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you Catholic now? Mm-hmm. Did you convert him, or was it...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I converted when he got to about 30, 40 years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Or is he not converted?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was too busy before that. Was he?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Has the church played an important role in your life? Oh, yes. Have you always... or before, were you always involved with church activities?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. When you were younger?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: As a child?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we went to school. When we came from Wisconsin and went to Coeur d'Alene, we went to the Catholic school there. They don't have one there anymore, but they had one when we moved there, and we went to the Catholic school for four years, so it made a lot of difference. And then they didn't have one in St. Mary's when we came up here, but they finally got one. It was here for about 40 years, and then it's gone now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, but they did have the Catholic school. Did you say you chose?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All our children went to the Catholic school. It was a grade school, not a high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are all of them still Catholic?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were they married to Catholics or... Well, there's...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, Bill over there, that girl, joined the church afterwards, and John, his wife didn't join, but she went to church with him. Lucille's husband joined the church the same time Jane did, and Frances Ann's husband joined the church after they were married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's pretty good. What suggestions would you make to give a young woman who has decided to live on a farm or in a small town? Or would you make any?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you feel...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Everybody would want to live on a farm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, if somebody had decided that they wanted to do that, would you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, I think they would.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there any particular advice you might give them to kind of help them make the change?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you feel pretty independent? I mean, do you feel as though you could do without a lot of monitoring and assistance?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you make your own soap or have you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I haven't made soap. I haven't made soap. I got arrested, but I haven't made it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your mother make soap? Uh-huh. Did you ever help her?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. I think she made that soap and... Well, she might have made it over here when she was over here in this boarding house, too, you know, because... But she had a lot of help in that boarding house. It was a big deal. That was a big meal, and she had a lot of men there. And so she had a cook, a man cook there. So I suppose it wasn't anything that I would do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Did you help your mother at the boarding house? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Waited tables and laid beds.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about your mother's and sister's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my sister, the older sister did, too. I don't think they've always been much. Ha ha ha.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They didn't do much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Oh, maybe they packed in wood. There must have been wood. In those days, they used wood. They had great big stoves that they... Maybe they did. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you waited on tables. How did you like waiting on tables?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it was all right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Describe your life and how the depression affected it, or did it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we had a hard time, but we got by.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. The depression occurred after you were married, right? Yeah. So you were living here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We were living in town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was your husband doing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was a little bit in the woods. He worked in the woods a long time when he was gone.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the depression hurt the lumber business? It didn't?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you remained working all that time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Most of the time, he was doing something. He built roads with his brother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it really hard for you? Were you one of the luckier families? No, no.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was hard, but then we had a cow and pig in the garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did that make a big difference?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, sure it did. We had a bunch of children and you had milk. You know you had milk. Chickens. We had chickens. So we didn't live... At that time, the part of town we lived in was not part of the state. It had been an annex right now, but it wasn't a state.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I have no idea what it was like during the depression. What happened during the war? How did the war affect your life? Start with World War I and then talk about World War II.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know that World War I... I worked at the dog and that's when I was over in my home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your job have anything to do with the war effort?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was a bookstore. I was working in a store.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that business helped or hurt by the war?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm not sure. It was a little town where there was only that one store.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why did you live over there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when I got through school, they gave you a choice to go to school. So they had that job. That job was open and I went.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about World War II? How did that affect your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just that... The war too, like one boy, the boy that's here, went to... was in the army, but they sent him to Texas and he couldn't prosper so they gave him a medical discharge. The other boy was in the Navy and he went to... he was overseas. And I suppose that...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I could have a brush in there. I know Jim was working up there in the logging once, if you remember, during the war, when you would go to Spain to get groceries, pay the workers. That was during the Depression. Oh, that was during the Depression. Yeah, that's right, because you were out here when things were easy. Yeah, he was... during the Depression he was logging and he took his logs down to Springsteen and they took out those people. They had traded... they had a store and they traded for groceries. So, I'm...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. I don't belong.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Has your dependence on the grocery store changed? Oh...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All of them used to be staples. We have lots of vegetables in there that are frozen and it doesn't take... For instance, in... I put in... For a piece, like, I would put two packages in a quart box and that would be... one package in a... that would be in a self-embracing... would be... would be enough for a meal. So, and we had all kinds of... I think the peas... we're out of peas now. We didn't have that many peas at that time. But... so, we had a lot of things that... Lots of things we didn't have to buy. Carrots, squash... Carrots and squash. We had a squash last week that we raised last summer. That's the longest we've kept them in the wintertime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, we just found a little acorn squash that was about this big and it had turned orange that we just ate. We didn't grow it. Bruce's dad did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, those are nice squashes. So... Outside meat, we don't have meat. We were out of meat yesterday. There was meat there, she says. Until now. It's gone through the weather tonight.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does your husband have? Hmm? Does your husband have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't have any more. Me too. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of meat did you get there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Venison.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Deer, elk, both? Deer, yeah. Any moose? No. I think that's really interesting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We have a son that lives over here across the river. He used to get elk and bring elk out here, you know. Yeah, we just don't have a lot of that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever make sausage or anything like that? No. Just frozen meat? Mm-hmm. Do you butcher your own?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we don't butcher our own. We get it from down there. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long has it been since you've raised any cattle or pigs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, since we moved up here. We haven't had any cattle or any pigs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it just space or was it just too informative?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it's just we just fed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Okay, what magazines and newspapers does your family subscribe to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: U.S. News & World Report, The Greater Digest, The Grit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you seen The Grit? You can prove it there. I may have proved it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's a good magazine. What type of magazine is it? Oh, it has everything in it. Everything in it. And I get the U.S. News & World Report. No, I don't get that. I get The Greater Digest, The Good Housekeeping, The American Heritage, and The Sky Post.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that what your neighbor... Does she make the tapes of those?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She makes the tapes of the St. Mary's paper, St. Mary's Gazette.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But the others you subscribe to that way?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I subscribe to them. Yeah, I subscribe to them. They come from Boise.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think I've heard of that sort of thing before.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, they have a... They send out a... Oh, what they call a talking book copy. And it's a little... Well, I don't know, kind of a...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Whether it's...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What kind of... It's a record. And it tells you... It gives you the number of the book and tells you what the book is about. And they send a paper that has it all listed in order blank. It's all listed. All the books are listed. And you just listen to that little record and take your choice of books. And they send... Once a year they send out a catalog. And sometimes when I get lazy I don't write St. Mary's. And they just send me what books they want. But they've been doing pretty good lately because... I like books... Oh, I like... Books about... Like the book we have right now is called... About coming to North... Coming West to... For the Gold Rush in California. That's one of the books.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it's just nice. There's so many books. I like the older books, though. There's some of the... Some of the new books.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type... Have your taste in books changed over the years?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think so. I don't know. If I could get all the books I wanted to, the older books... You know, I used to read books by Kathleen Norris. And they were all always homey books, you know. By home, most of the time. But I got one not long ago that was altogether different. It was altogether different versions of books Kathleen Norris used to read.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you like novels or big... Autobiographies? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You can get any kind. You can get any kind of books you want. There's adult fiction, adult nonfiction... History, religion, geography...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which ones do you like the best?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I like these... I haven't taken too many of the... Like the history and the old books. Geography and books. I like the... I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you watch TV very much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not very much anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What types of programs have you watched?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, most of the time we watch this... Watch the... What's My Line and Tell the Truth. Hollywood Squares. But there's so many stories on there that are just absolutely no good. And we watch the Waltons. And usually on Sunday night we watch... Royal Kingdom and Walt Disney.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What's your favorite Disney show?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And Welk. I watch Welk too. What's my favorite one? Yeah. My favorite one? I like the Waltons and Royal Kingdom. But I never watch the TV and Daytime anymore. I used to. But... And we watch a show, you know, to see what's going to be. And if we don't like it, we just turn it off. But there's so many shows. There's so much... Oh, I don't know. So many shows with all these great stories. I don't know why we still don't know all of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever go to the movies in town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We don't have a movie here. It's at the corner. We haven't had a movie house here for a long, long time. The people that had the movie house here years ago, and they had a long time, they fixed it so nobody else could get a movie show in this town. Now they really need one because anybody that would do it would be good for St. Mary's. But they don't have one. They, the Sun, started an outdoor movie at Plummer. Quite a while ago. I don't know whether it's open yet, and it just runs in the summertime. But somebody really should have a bedroom at St. Mary's because I'm sure St. Mary's is so nice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, here's a good one. Thinking back, what are the most common things your husband asks you about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, dear.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isn't that a good question?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's a good question.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are you asking me, Jane? I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What kind of pie did I make today?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you bake pies? Or do you usually bake pies every day?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. Because one pie, and I make smaller pies now than I used to. And sometimes I don't use it because I might eat a little bit less.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When the children were growing up, did you bake pies all the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, not every day. Lots of milk to make puddings with, and lots of eggs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you make pudding from scratch?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. And cake from scratch. I never use it. I hardly ever use it in the house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, he's been asking, what kind of bread do you make?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I mostly make white bread. And I make rolls that my grandkids just love. Just plain rolls. We can go over there to dinner and take a pan of rolls, and that's all they want. They don't care whether they got the rest of the meal or not. Just the rolls.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's great. Let's see. No, that's not a good question. Okay. When y'all had any big decisions to make, were they joint decisions?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Not like they try to tell families to do now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, what about just you and your husband as a couple?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, we used to do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you always done that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you decided to raise a family, was that... Did y'all just both have decided you wanted a family, and you just started having children? Did you plan when you wanted your children? No. No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They just came.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything else that you would like to tell me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you compare your life with your mother's life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my mother was a businesswoman. No, I wasn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you say that you're happier than she was, or were you both happier before she died?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I think I'm happier than she was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you sure?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I'm not sure. I'm not sure. But that's what she liked. That's what she liked. And she really was a good one. A good businesswoman. And I'm not. Compared to... I wouldn't want to go out and run a house. But, um... Well, she had the Kootenaian one before... When she retired, she was... She had the Kootenaian for several years. And I wouldn't want that kind of work at all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she find any conflict between running a business and raising children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't think so. Because her youngsters were involved. When she came to... Well, when she came to... When we came from Cardell Lane, the youngest girl was just a little... The youngest one was just a little girl. You know, like, she was just starting school. And that man that ran the... Had the mill that he built over there, he set up a school where there was oh, maybe just three or four grades, you know. That's where she started school. So, um... Oh, I don't know. I don't know. I think my mother really enjoyed that kind of work. I wouldn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she... Did your mother seem to be a really happy person most of the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I think she was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And she ran the boarding house before your father died, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, uh-huh. And then they went to... Well, she ran another hotel here. It's called the Valley... Well, they also run a confectionery store here. It's down on... It's on Main Street. She run that for a long time, the two of them. And then they went to Davenport, Washington and had a confectionery store over there. And when she came back to St. Mary's, she bought that recruitment in mind.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you compare your mother's way of raising children to your way?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. It was like mine. Mine, I was with them all the time, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And, uh...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course, she wasn't when we were in Coeur d'Alene. No, in Coeur d'Alene, she worked. Her sister owned a big... owned a boarding house for the Blackwell mill. And we lived with her a while, but then we lived in a place of our own. And when we lived like that, well, she was always with us, but we were grown enough, you know, like I was in... Well, no, my brothers were in the grade school when we came to St. Mary's, and my sister was an eighth grader. And I was in the ninth grader, so she was... Except that youngest one was still a little girl. She was ten years younger than me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your mother's working have... What effect did that have on you as a child?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't think it had any effect. It was just... Because we had lots of... We had lots of things. We had lots of... And, uh... We worked in the dining room, my sister and I, but... We had lots of nice clothes. And we went to school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever consider working after you got married, or after the children were gone? Yeah, I did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I helped my mother in the Kootenai Inn with the bookkeeping,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: but that's all I did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's the only place I ever went.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you've always been happy here at home? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I have.
